newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court issues temporary stay of new phone rules.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court issues temporary stay of new phone rules.

text.p: A U.S. appeals court in St. Louis put a temporary freeze Friday on landmark federal rules designed to pry open the $100 billion local phone market to long-distance carriers, cable-television operators and others.

The Federal Communications Commission's landmark regulations were to go into effect Monday, but have been challenged by local phone companies, the regional Baby Bells and state regulators who are seeking to overturn them.

The court issued a stay of the rules until next Thursday when oral argument will be heard about whether to put the rules on ice until a final ruling is made in the case. A final ruling is expected in 1997. A long stay would be a major blow to the FCC as well as long-distance carriers such a AT&T Corp. who are trying to break into the local market.
Attorney Alfred Mamlet of Steptoe & Johnson said the latest stay, while temporary, is important because courts often dismiss such requests for a stay "without argument."
Those challenging the rules were elated. "We're encouraged that the court is taking a close look at these onerous rules," said BellSouth Corp. spokesman Bill McCloskey.
"It demonstrates to us that the court sees enough of a problem that they feel they should move to oral arguments."

But rival AT&T, in a statement, called the court's decision "purely procedural. It is designed only to permit sufficient time for the court to hear oral arguments on whether a long stay should be granted."

Local and regional phone companies as well as state regulators argue that the FCC overstepped its authority when implementing a key provision of the telecommunications law passed by Congress earlier this year.
They took the matter to court after the FCC in August approved the rules, which involve nationwide standards for how the local markets should be opened.
The Bells and state regulators argued against national standards. The rules, for example, require the Bells to lease their local phone lines to rivals at steep discounts.
Long-distance carriers and other rivals to the Bells, meanwhile, applauded the rules.
"It is perfectly reasonable for the court to want to hear oral argument in this case. We continue to be confident that our position will prevail," said FCC Chairman Reed Hundt.
Next week's arguments will involve local phone companies, state regulators, the Bells, the FCC and rivals trying to break into the local market.

The various cases challenging the rules were filed around the country and then consolidated with the U.S. appeals court in St. Louis. Next week's arugments will be heard in a U.S. appeals court in Kansas City, Mo.
